card: An active participle is a verb used as an adjective: **челове́к, чита́ющий газе́ту** = *the man reading the paper*. Present: the **они́** form minus **-т** + **-щий** (**чита́ют → чита́ющий**). Past: the past stem + **-вший** (**прочита́л → прочита́вший**). They decline like adjectives and belong mostly to writing; in speech say **кото́рый чита́ет**.

sections.body: Participles let written Russian pack a whole clause into one word. News, instructions and literature use them constantly; conversation prefers **кото́рый**. At B2 you need to recognise them; at C1, to produce the common ones.

rows: **-вший** after a vowel, **-ший** after a consonant

sections.title: Aspect and tense
sections.body: Present participles come only from imperfective verbs: **чита́ющий** (*who is reading*). Past participles come from both aspects: **чита́вший** (*who was reading*), **прочита́вший** (*who has read*). Reflexive verbs keep **-ся**, even after a vowel: **занима́ющийся**, **верну́вшийся**.

sections.title: Agreement
sections.body: The participle agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, like any adjective: **Я говори́л с челове́ком, чита́ющим газе́ту.** **Мы ви́дели студе́нтов, сдаю́щих экза́мен.** A participle phrase after its noun is set off by commas.

English uses *-ing* for several things that Russian keeps apart. *The man reading* is a participle (**чита́ющий**); *while reading* is a gerund (**чита́я**); *reading is useful* is an infinitive or a noun (**чита́ть поле́зно**, **чте́ние**).

mistakes.why: No present participle from a perfective verb: use the past, **прочита́вший**.
Participles always keep **-ся**, even after a vowel.

examples.en: The man reading the paper is my neighbour.
The students taking the exam are very nervous.

examples.ru: Я встре́тил дру́га, верну́вшегося из Москвы́.
examples.en: I met a friend who had come back from Moscow.

examples.ru: Э́то расска́з о де́вочке, потеря́вшей соба́ку.
examples.en: It's a story about a girl who lost her dog.
A tourist who spoke Russian helped us.
